environmental_signs: Season of the young. The rains ease and the weather warms, with easterly winds in the morning and cooling sea breezes in the afternoon. This was the time for mosaic burning, which reduced fuel, created grazing pasture, helped seeds germinate and made it easier to move across country. Fledglings are leaving their nests, reptiles are shedding their skin, and baby frogs are completing their transformation into adults.

Season of adolescence. This is the hottest, driest part of the year, with hot easterlies and a sea breeze on most afternoons near the coast. Traditionally people lived by the coast, rivers and estuaries, so seafood and freshwater foods were a big part of the diet. White gum flowers (Jarrah, Marri, Ghost Gum) are in bloom, and the female Zamia's seeds ripen from green to red, which draws in emus.

Season of adult. The intense heat finally breaks, and cool, dewy nights signal the change. Winds turn light and southerly, flying ants appear, and red flowers (Red-flowering Gum, Summer Flame) show up as the Banksias begin to bloom. Foods included stored Zamia seeds, Yanget bulbs, fish, frogs and turtles. As nights turned damp, mia mias (shelters) were repaired to be waterproof before winter.

Season of fertility. This is the coldest and wettest time of the year, with westerly and southerly winds, and occasional snow on the Stirling and Porongurup Ranges. People traditionally moved inland as waterways filled, shifting from sea foods to land animals such as kangaroo, whose skins became "bookas" (cloaks) and whose bones and sinews were made into tools. Animals pair up to breed, with ravens flying in pairs and Mali (Black Swans) arriving on lakes and rivers to nest.

Season of conception. Djilba is a transitional season mixing cold, clear days with warm, rainy, windy ones. It begins the big wildflower explosion in the south-west, starting with yellow Acacias, then cream and vivid blue flowers. Land animals like kangaroo, emu and possum remained key foods, and the first newborns appear. Nesting woodland birds, like magpies, swoop to protect their young, and Balga (Grass Tree) flower stalks start to emerge.

Season of birth. Kambarang is the second spring, a time of transformation with flowers everywhere, including Acacias, Banksias, Kangaroo Paw and orchids. The Mooja (Christmas Tree) blooms in bright orange-yellow, signalling that the heat is coming. Snakes wake from hibernation, so October is the most likely time to see one, and baby birds call for food while magpies guard their nests. Dry spells get longer as the weather warms.
